basics.name: Western woodworking joint books: The Joint Book: The Complete Guide to Wood Joinery (Terrie Noll; UK title Woodworker's Joint Book) and The Complete Illustrated Guide to Joinery (Gary Rogowski, Taunton Press)
basics.url: No single home page. Noll: Open Library work https://openlibrary.org/works/OL8551662W (US/Australian editions) and Internet Archive lending copy of the UK edition https://archive.org/details/woodworkersjoint0000noll ; Google Books record with contents highlights https://books.google.com/books/about/The_Joint_Book.html?id=Z7zZAAAAMAAJ . Rogowski: publisher page (Abrams, which now sells Taunton books) https://www.abramsbooks.com/product/complete-illustrated-guide-to-joinery_9781561584017/ ; Internet Archive lending copy https://archive.org/details/completeillustra0000rogo ; Google Books record https://books.google.com/books/about/The_Complete_Illustrated_Guide_to_Joiner.html?id=W_1TAAAAMAAJ
basics.resource_type: book (two illustrated how-to catalogues of Western wood joints, each organised as a joint classification by family)
basics.cost: Paid. Noll: listed at USD 25.99 (Barnes & Noble, spiral-bound hardcover, out of stock online when checked); cheap used copies common. Rogowski: USD 49.99 list, hardcover (Abrams); used copies about USD 20 to 36 (ThriftBooks). Both can be borrowed free (one reader at a time) from Internet Archive's lending library with a free account
basics.license: All rights reserved (commercial publishers: Popular Woodworking Books / Apple Press / Chartwell for Noll; Taunton Press for Rogowski). Link to the book records and cite page numbers; do not copy the drawings or photos into the encyclopedia
basics.language: English (Noll's UK edition uses British spellings such as 'mitres'; US editions use 'miters')
basics.year: Noll: The Joint Book first published 2002 (Apple Press UK, 'Woodworker's Joint Book', Nov 2002; Popular Woodworking Books US, Jan 2003; Gary Allen, Australia, Dec 2002); Chartwell reprint 30 Jan 2007; Apple Press reissue 2007. Noll's earlier, shorter 'The Encyclopedia of Jointmaking' (144 pages) came out in 1997, and The Joint Book appears to expand it [uncertain]. Rogowski: first and only edition 15 Jan 2002 (Taunton), still in print from Abrams in 2026
basics.access_barrier: Paywall (buy the book), or a free Internet Archive login to borrow the access-restricted scan. No open full text
basics.image_license: All rights reserved. Noll uses drawn step-by-step illustrations plus photos; Rogowski uses over 1,400 colour photographs and drawings owned by Taunton Press
basics.authority_level: Educator/professional. Noll is a former editor of Woodwork magazine with over 20 years as a furniture designer and maker (Google Books author note). Rogowski is a master furniture maker who founded the Northwest Woodworking Studio in Portland, Oregon (building furniture since 1974) and is a regular Fine Woodworking contributor (Abrams and Google Books author notes). Not peer-reviewed

coverage.covers: Hand-made and machine-made joints for solid wood and sheet goods in furniture and cabinet work. Noll (192 pages, spiral-bound so it lies flat on the bench): 'over 70 joints' with step-by-step illustrated instructions for hand tools and power tools, grouped into edge and scarf joints, lapped and housed joints, mortise-and-tenon joints, mitres and bevels, dovetails, and dowels and biscuits, plus a chapter on assembly fasteners and reinforcements covering hardware and knock-down (take-apart) joints, an intro on wood, joint design and glues, and a glossary. Rogowski (390 to 400 pages, large format): 'every practical woodworking joint' from simple butt joints to angled tenons and complex scarf joints, in over 1,400 step-by-step photos; typically several alternative methods per joint (hand tool, router, tablesaw, biscuit joiner). Exact joint count for Rogowski not published; roughly 80 to 100 named joints and variants [uncertain]
coverage.organisation: Both are organised by joint family, then by variant, then by method. Noll: introduction (wood as a material, joint design, glues and gluing, clamping and assembly) then one chapter per joint family, plus a quick-reference 'Joint Selector' guide at the front for picking a joint by job. Rogowski: Part One on tools (hand tools, portable power tools, machines), then joints split by what you are building: carcase joinery (boxes and cabinets: butt, rabbet, groove, dado, miter, finger, dovetail joints), frame joinery (doors and tables: miter, lap, bridle, mortise-and-tenon, scarf and splice joints) and edge joints. Each section opens with a visual map (thumbnail photo contents) of the joints in it, so you can find a joint by picture. The carcase/frame split is useful for beginners because it starts from what you are making, not from joint names; but the chapter names themselves (rabbet, dado, bridle) are jargon
coverage.scope_match: medium. Woodworking joinery is an in-scope family (lowest priority by making method), and both books are thorough, well-illustrated catalogues of joint TYPES with strong coverage of the clever ones (sliding dovetails, wedged and tusk tenons, drawbored tenons, knock-down joints). But they cover only wood, give no 3D-printing, CNC-specific or mechanism content, and most of their joints are glued and permanent rather than 'special behaviour' connections
coverage.taxonomy_used: Western joint families. Noll: about 7 top-level groups (edge and scarf; lapped and housed; mortise and tenon; mitres and bevels; dovetails; dowels and biscuits; fasteners, hardware and knock-down joints). Rogowski: 3 top-level groups by construction type (carcase joinery, frame joinery, edge joints) after a tools part, subdivided into joint families (butt, knock-down, rabbet/groove/dado, miter, finger, dovetail, mortise and tenon, lap, bridle, scarf/splice, edge). Section numbers seen in search snippets (e.g. Section 4 butt joints, Section 8 halved joints) suggest around 15 to 20 sections [uncertain]
coverage.example_types: Sliding dovetail (a dovetail-shaped tongue slid into a matching groove; locks in one direction) [Rogowski index, uncertain]; tusk tenon (a through tenon locked by a loose removable wedge, knock-down; Rogowski shows wedge designs on p.149 per a Sawmill Creek reader) [uncertain]; wedged through tenon; drawbored tenon (offset peg hole pulls the joint tight, needs no clamps) [Noll]; haunched mortise and tenon [Noll]; loose (floating) tenon; bridle joint (open mortise); half-lap and cross-lap (halved joints); housed / dado and shouldered dado; drawer lock joint and dado rabbet; tongue and groove and loose tongue (spline); splined and keyed mitre; finger (box) joint; through, half-blind and secret mitred dovetails; scarf joint (end-to-end splice); biscuit and dowel joints; knock-down joints and hardware (e.g. bed bolts, cross dowels, knock-down fittings) [Noll chapter; exact list uncertain]. Rogowski's knock-down section (p.56) and the drawer lock, loose tongue and dado rabbet sections (pp.93 to 103) were seen only in search snippets, not on an opened page [uncertain]
coverage.making_methods: Woodwork only: hand tools (saw, chisel, plane) and power tools (router, tablesaw, biscuit joiner, drill jigs). Rogowski adds machines. No 3D printing, CNC programming, laser cutting or metal
coverage.item_count: Noll: over 70 joints (publisher blurb). Rogowski: 1,400+ photos and diagrams; joint count not stated, roughly 80 to 100 joints and variants [uncertain]
coverage.special_behaviours_covered: Knock-down / hand-release (take-apart joints: tusk tenons, bed bolts, knock-down fittings) and self-locking by shape or wedging (sliding dovetails, wedged and drawbored tenons, dovetails that only come apart in one direction). Adhesives: both cover wood glues and gluing technique (Noll has a 'Glues and Gluing' section; typical coverage is PVA/yellow glue, hide glue, epoxy and similar wood glues [uncertain]). Not covered: torque-limiting, one-way/ratchet, indexing/detent, over-centre, compliant, print-in-place, gear trains, powered connectors
coverage.entry_structure: Noll: joint name, short description of use and strength, exploded or assembled drawing, then numbered step-by-step illustrated instructions for hand and power tool methods, with variations. Rogowski: joint overview with a drawing, 'choosing the joint' notes, then photo essays of several methods (each step a captioned photo), tips and warnings. Neither has CAD files, animations or degrees-of-freedom notes
coverage.audience_level: Hobbyist to professional woodworker (Noll: beginners and experienced woodworkers; Rogowski: aimed at intermediate to advanced woodworkers but usable by committed beginners)

usefulness.beginner_friendliness: medium to high. Noll is small, spiral-bound and step-by-step, with a Joint Selector up front, so a beginner can go from job to joint to method. Rogowski is very visual (1,400+ photos, visual-map contents) but long and uses standard woodworking jargon (rabbet, dado, haunch, carcase) without much plain-English framing
usefulness.has_images: yes. Noll: clear line drawings for every step plus photos. Rogowski: over 1,400 full-colour photos and drawings, high quality
usefulness.gaps: Wood only, and mostly permanent glued joints. No coverage of 3D-printed or CNC-cut adaptations (clearances for printed dovetails, laser-cut finger joints, etc.). No motion-type or 'special behaviour' index (you cannot look up 'joints that come apart by hand'). Few numbers on strength. Paywalled and all rights reserved, so images cannot be reused. Jargon-heavy family names give a beginner no way in unless they already know what a 'housed' or 'bridle' joint is
usefulness.good_for_entry_links: poor for per-entry links. Books have no per-joint URLs; the best you can do is cite the book record (e.g. https://archive.org/details/completeillustra0000rogo) with a page number
usefulness.reusable_data: not reusable. No dataset or API; the family structure (joint families and their names) can be used as a reference taxonomy, but the text and images are all rights reserved
usefulness.maintained: Static print books. Noll last reprinted 2007 (out of stock at Barnes & Noble when checked); Rogowski 2002 edition still sold new by Abrams in 2026. Both borrowable on Internet Archive
usefulness.ideas_to_borrow: (1) A front-of-book 'Joint Selector' (Noll): pick your job first, then the joint. (2) Split by what you are building (Rogowski's carcase vs frame vs edge), which maps well to a flow chart question such as 'Are you joining boards side by side, making a box corner, or making a frame corner?'. (3) Visual map at the start of each section: a grid of small pictures of every joint in the family, so readers pick by look not by name. (4) Show several ways to make each joint with different tools (hand, router, tablesaw), which maps to the project's 'making method' filter. (5) Spiral-bound, workshop-friendly short entries (Noll)
usefulness.design_rules_given: Some woodworking rules of thumb, e.g. tenon thickness about one third of stock thickness, grain direction and wood movement considerations, glue surface (long grain vs end grain) [uncertain: seen in general joinery coverage, not verified page by page]. No engineering load tables
usefulness.file_formats: Print book (Noll spiral-bound hardcover; Rogowski hardcover); Internet Archive lending scans (PDF/EPUB, access-restricted); Kindle edition of Rogowski may exist [uncertain]
usefulness.terminology_value: good for standard Western (US and UK) woodworking joint names and variants (e.g. housed vs dado, mitre vs miter, bridle vs open mortise), with Noll's glossary. Not a source for translations
usefulness.decision_support: Noll has a quick-reference 'Joint Selector' guide (a chart matching joints to typical jobs; exact layout not verified [uncertain]). Rogowski helps readers choose joints by function, time, skill level and tools (publisher blurb) and groups joints by carcase vs frame use, but has no flow chart
usefulness.derived_from_or_overlaps: Noll's The Joint Book appears to build on her 1997 'The Encyclopedia of Jointmaking' [uncertain]. Rogowski's book is part of Taunton's Complete Illustrated Guides series (companion volumes on furniture and cabinet construction and shaping wood) and overlaps heavily with Fine Woodworking magazine articles (same publisher; Rogowski writes for Fine Woodworking). Both overlap with Wikipedia's joinery tables and Wood Magazine / Fine Woodworking online joint guides; readers also recommend Sam Allen's Wood Joiner's Handbook as an alternative (Sawmill Creek thread https://sawmillcreek.org/threads/exposed-joinery-tusk-tenons.13992/)
